summary:
American Samoa's criminal law does not punish consensual sodomy. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, criminalised male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian sex. The Fono's 1979 revision of the criminal law, which took effect in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and persons unable to give consent. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

American Samoa stands under the national framework of the United States as an unorganised and unincorporated territory. The federal layer covering passports, identity documents and federal agency practice is carried by the parent record for the United States and is not restated here.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed in American Samoa, which the record describes as the only jurisdiction in the United States, apart from certain tribal jurisdictions, that does not issue such licences. In July 2015 Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale was reviewing whether the United States Supreme Court's marriage-equality ruling applied to the territory and said at the time that applicability was still under review. The Governor stated that the ruling did not apply, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed a licence application in July 2015, and the 2026 law review article records that none has applied since.

On 20 March 2003 the Fono Senate rejected a bill introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster that would have outlawed same-sex marriage, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The territory therefore declined to enact a statutory ban before the 2015 national ruling.

In January 2016 the Senate confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as a District Court judge. Asked at his confirmation hearing by Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, whether he had read the 2015 marriage decision, Sunia replied that he had not, that the district court does not deal with the ruling, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change. Eighteen months after the ruling, the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that it did not automatically apply.

The operative legal position remains contested in the sources. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that the 2015 ruling does apply despite local officials' statements, and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; it sets out a litigation route through the High Court of American Samoa, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, and then the US Department of the Interior. A July 2024 on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, tested whether the local same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment, which treats its constitutional durability as an open question and indicates that the ban is treated as operative locally. Because no couple has applied, no court has ruled.

Marriages performed elsewhere must be recognised in American Samoa: since 13 December 2022 the Respect for Marriage Act has required all territories, including American Samoa, to recognise same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples, without obliging the territory to perform them.

On identity documents, the Office of Vital Statistics may change the gender marker on an American Samoa birth certificate where medical documentation of a sex change is presented, and will change the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order. The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates should be altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, and the Office has interpreted that ruling to cover applications from transgender individuals.

Three documented 2023 matters concern trans people directly. In June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity, and in September 2023 the US Department of Justice secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen. These are the only trans-specific incidents dated in this record; no later instance is documented.

Socially, American Samoan society is described as highly religious, with conservative attitudes regarding gender and sexuality tending to dominate, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. At the same time fa'afafine, boys raised in a female role within Samoan communal life, are a recognised part of local culture, and the record describes American Samoa as tending to be tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities.
tangentialFactors:
Fa'afafine identity carries explicit cultural standing in American Samoa. The UH Manoa research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 23 July 2026, defines fa'afafine as people born male who embody both male and female traits and describes the identity as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, framed against colonial suppression and contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, re-anchored to cultural pride. It is the territory's main LGBTQ organisation and runs annual events and festivals and campaigns for the betterment of the fa'afafine community. The first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei, with pageant, song, dance and poetry choral competitions; beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community are popular and families generally attend in support of candidates.

Public comportment is restrained regardless of orientation. A 2009 Out Traveler column by Ed Salvato described reserved behaviour by people of all orientations as expected in American Samoa, while characterising homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture and contrasting the territory with Fiji, where it described homophobia as rampant. The same column reported that local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands the homeland of fa'afafine culture, and noted that hotels in the territory skew toward business travel.

Local fa'afafine opinion on marriage was recorded in the 2003 legislative hearing. Fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine do not believe in marriages with other men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, and citing Christian upbringing. The 2024 constitutional survey likewise probes cultural dimensions bearing on the marriage question, including collectivistic versus individualistic orientation and linear versus polychronic time.

The Office of Vital Statistics applies that ruling to applications from transgender individuals: it changes the name when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

Employment exposure for trans residents has produced two documented legal outcomes in 2023. The 2026 law review article by two local attorneys concludes that it applies and that a certificate must be issued to any applicant; the July 2024 on-island survey treats the local ban as operative and its survival under the 14th Amendment as an open question; the January 2016 judicial exchange shows the district court proceeding as if the ruling did not bind it. The federal layer on passports, gender markers and executive orders reaching US territories is not sourced at region level in this inventory and is carried by the parent record for the United States.

No region-specific data is sourced on airport screening, document flagging or secondary inspection at Pago Pago for transgender travellers, and none is asserted here.

No trans-specific violence rate with a denominator exists for the territory in this inventory. The February 2023 charge involving a 16-year-old transgender teen is a single documented case and does not establish a prevalence level; no later trans-specific incident is dated in this record.
